title: Dubai or Abu Dhabi: Which Is Better for Your Family?
content:
If you are planning to move to the UAE with your family, one of the biggest decisions you may face is whether to live in Dubai or Abu Dhabi.

Both cities offer excellent schools, beautiful beaches, safe communities, modern healthcare and plenty of family activities. However, the experience of living in each city can feel very different.

After living in Dubai for more than 12 years, I recently moved to Abu Dhabi with my husband and daughters. However, I still work in Dubai and commute between the two cities every working day.

This may sound like a huge journey to someone new to the UAE, but commuting between Abu Dhabi and Dubai is very doable. Many people live in one emirate and work in the other. Whether the commute works for you will depend heavily on where you live, where you work and the times you need to travel.

Dubai was my home for a very long time, and it will always be an important part of my story. Abu Dhabi is now where we have chosen to build our family life, while Dubai remains a major part of my professional life.

So, which city is better for your family?

The honest answer is that it depends on the lifestyle you want, your budget, your children’s schools and how your family feels about commuting.

Dubai and Abu Dhabi at a Glance

If your family wants...

Consider...

A faster, busier lifestyle

Dubai

A calmer pace of life

Abu Dhabi

A wider public transport network

Dubai

More space and a quieter atmosphere

Abu Dhabi

Constant events and new openings

Dubai

Easy access to beaches and island life

Abu Dhabi

A very large choice of communities

Dubai

A capital-city lifestyle that feels less hectic

Abu Dhabi

More nightlife and dining variety

Dubai

Relaxed family weekends and outdoor spaces

Abu Dhabi

To live in Abu Dhabi while continuing a Dubai career

Both, with a daily commute

This is only a general guide. Your experience will depend heavily on the neighbourhood you choose. Some parts of Dubai feel quiet and suburban, while some areas of Abu Dhabi are busy, lively and full of activity.

The Overall Lifestyle

Living in Dubai

Dubai is exciting, ambitious and always moving.

There is constantly a new restaurant opening, an event happening or an attraction to visit. The city is filled with people from around the world, and it can feel as though everything you could possibly need is available.

For families who enjoy being busy, exploring new places and having endless entertainment options, Dubai can be incredible.

However, the pace can also feel intense. Traffic, commuting, busy calendars and the pressure to keep up with everything happening around you can become tiring.

Dubai is a city where it is very easy to be constantly doing something.

Living in Abu Dhabi

Abu Dhabi feels calmer, more spacious and slightly more relaxed.

It is still a modern international city with restaurants, shopping centres, schools, attractions and beautiful hotels, but the overall pace feels less rushed.

Since moving to Abu Dhabi, I have noticed that family life feels a little slower. There is more of a sense that you can step back, breathe and enjoy your surroundings without feeling that you are missing out on ten other things.

That does not mean Abu Dhabi is boring. Yas Island, Saadiyat Island, Hudayriyat Island, the Corniche and the city’s cultural attractions provide plenty to do. The difference is that the city generally feels less hectic.

For our family, Abu Dhabi gives us a calmer home life while my daily commute allows me to remain connected to my work in Dubai.

Housing and Family Communities

Both Dubai and Abu Dhabi offer apartments, villas, gated communities and waterfront living.

Housing in Dubai

Dubai has an enormous variety of communities. Families can choose between city apartments, beachfront locations, established villa communities and newer suburban developments.

Popular family areas include Arabian Ranches, Dubai Hills, Jumeirah, Mirdif, The Springs, The Meadows, Town Square and many more.

The advantage of Dubai is choice. The disadvantage is that choosing the wrong location can lead to a very long daily commute.

A beautiful villa on one side of the city may not feel so perfect when school and work are on the other side.

Housing in Abu Dhabi

Abu Dhabi also offers a wide choice of family communities, although the city feels more compact in some areas.

Families may consider locations such as Khalifa City, Al Raha, Yas Island, Saadiyat Island, Reem Island, Al Reef, Al Mushrif and the Corniche area.

Depending on the location and budget, you may find that Abu Dhabi offers more space or a quieter environment. However, premium island communities and waterfront properties can still be very expensive.

If you plan to work in Dubai, the location of your Abu Dhabi home becomes especially important. Living closer to the main route between the two cities can make the daily journey much easier.

My Advice

Do not choose your home until you understand where everyone needs to be each day.

Check:

  • The morning drive to work
  • The school run
  • Afternoon traffic
  • Distance to supermarkets and medical facilities
  • Access to children’s activities
  • Parking
  • Nearby construction
  • Community facilities
  • Additional housing costs
  • Access to the main highway if you will commute between emirates

In both cities, location can affect your happiness more than the size or appearance of your home.

Schools and Education

Dubai and Abu Dhabi both have excellent international schools offering a variety of curriculums.

These can include:

  • British
  • American
  • International Baccalaureate
  • Australian
  • Indian
  • French
  • German
  • Canadian and other international programmes

Dubai has a particularly large selection of private schools, but popular schools may have waiting lists. Abu Dhabi also offers many established international schools and continues to expand its education options.

Families researching Dubai schools can use the KHDA school directory to compare schools, locations and available information. For Abu Dhabi, parents can explore private schools and fees through ADEK.

Do not select a school based only on its reputation. The best school is the one that suits your individual child and your family’s daily life.

Consider:

  • Curriculum
  • School inspection rating
  • Fees and additional charges
  • Distance from home
  • School transport
  • Class sizes
  • Learning support
  • Extracurricular activities
  • Communication with parents
  • The overall atmosphere during your visit

A highly rated school with a difficult two-hour daily school run may not be the best option for your family.

If one parent will be commuting between Abu Dhabi and Dubai, also think carefully about who will manage school drop-offs, collections, appointments and emergencies during the working day.

Getting Around

Transport in Dubai

Dubai has the more extensive public transport system of the two cities.

The Metro, Tram, buses, taxis and marine transport make it possible to live in certain areas without immediately buying a car. Communities located close to Metro stations can be particularly convenient for commuters.

Dubai’s official visitor guide provides an overview of the city’s public transport options.

However, public transport does not reach every residential community, and many families still choose to drive.

Traffic can be heavy, particularly during school and office hours. The location of your home, workplace and children’s school will make an enormous difference.

Transport in Abu Dhabi

Abu Dhabi has public buses and taxis, but many families find having a car more convenient.

The city is generally straightforward to navigate, with wide roads and many areas connected by bridges. Traffic still exists, especially around schools and during peak hours, but daily driving can feel less intense than in some parts of Dubai.

If you live, work and attend school within the same part of Abu Dhabi, your daily routine can be relatively manageable.

Commuting Between Abu Dhabi and Dubai

Living in Abu Dhabi does not automatically mean that you have to work in Abu Dhabi.

I live in Abu Dhabi with my family and commute to Dubai every working day. It is a significant journey, but it is completely manageable for me. It allows us to enjoy the family lifestyle we want in Abu Dhabi without giving up my career in Dubai.

Many UAE residents travel between the two emirates for work. Some live in Abu Dhabi and work in Dubai, while others make the journey in the opposite direction.

The commute becomes much easier when you choose your locations carefully. Living closer to the Dubai side of Abu Dhabi and working in an area with easy access to the main highway can make a huge difference.

Before deciding whether the commute is suitable for you, consider:

  • The exact location of your home
  • The exact location of your workplace
  • Your working hours
  • School drop-off and collection responsibilities
  • Traffic at the times you will travel
  • Fuel and road toll costs
  • Car mileage and maintenance
  • Whether your employer offers flexible or remote-working days
  • How much time you are comfortable spending in the car

Do not judge the journey only by the distance shown on a map. Test the actual route at the time you would normally travel.

For some people, the commute will feel too long. For others, including me, it is a worthwhile trade-off for being able to live in the city that best suits the family while continuing to work in Dubai.

Cost of Living

Neither Dubai nor Abu Dhabi should be considered a cheap city.

The cost of living in either location will depend on your housing, school choices, transport and lifestyle.

Your main expenses may include:

  • Rent
  • School fees
  • Nursery or childcare
  • Utilities
  • Air conditioning
  • Groceries
  • Medical insurance
  • Car payments and insurance
  • Fuel, parking and road tolls
  • Mobile phones and internet
  • Activities and entertainment
  • Dining out

Dubai can become particularly expensive if you choose a premium neighbourhood, attend high-fee schools and regularly participate in the city’s dining and entertainment scene.

Abu Dhabi may offer better value in certain areas, but premium communities such as Saadiyat and Yas Island can also carry high prices.

Rather than asking which city is cheaper, compare the actual lifestyle your family would have in each one.

Calculate the cost of:

  • A suitable family home
  • School fees
  • Daily transport
  • Medical insurance
  • The activities your family enjoys
  • Annual expenses paid upfront
  • Fuel, tolls and vehicle maintenance if you will commute

If you are considering living in Abu Dhabi and working in Dubai, compare the additional transport costs with what you may gain through your preferred home, community and family lifestyle.

The city with the lowest rent is not necessarily the city that will cost your family less overall.

Family Activities

You will not run out of things to do with children in either city.

Family Activities in Dubai

Dubai offers a huge variety of family entertainment, including:

  • Theme parks
  • Water parks
  • Indoor play centres
  • Beaches
  • Desert experiences
  • Museums
  • Aquariums
  • Sporting activities
  • Creative workshops
  • Seasonal events
  • Large shopping and entertainment destinations

Dubai is especially good for families who love trying new attractions and having a busy social calendar.

The amount of choice is fantastic, but family outings can quickly become expensive. It helps to mix the big-ticket attractions with beaches, parks and free community activities.

Family Activities in Abu Dhabi

Abu Dhabi offers a strong combination of entertainment, culture, beaches and outdoor experiences.

Family favourites include:

  • Warner Bros. World Abu Dhabi
  • Ferrari World Abu Dhabi
  • Yas Waterworld
  • SeaWorld Yas Island
  • The National Aquarium
  • Louvre Abu Dhabi
  • Saadiyat’s museums and cultural attractions
  • Corniche Beach
  • Hudayriyat Island
  • Mangrove kayaking
  • Parks and cycling tracks
  • Al Ain day trips

The official Experience Abu Dhabi family guide is a useful starting point for discovering activities across the emirate.

Abu Dhabi’s islands make it easy to combine a family activity with time outdoors, a beach visit or a relaxed meal.

Beaches and Outdoor Life

Both cities have beautiful beaches, but the experience can feel different.

Dubai offers famous beach destinations, beachfront restaurants, beach clubs and active waterfront communities. Places such as JBR, Kite Beach and Dubai Islands provide plenty of ways to enjoy the coast.

Abu Dhabi’s island layout makes the water feel like a natural part of the city. The Corniche, Saadiyat, Yas Island, Hudayriyat and Al Bateen offer beaches and waterfront spaces for different types of family days.

The Abu Dhabi Corniche includes eight kilometres of waterfront with walking and cycling paths, play areas, cafés and beach access, according to the official Abu Dhabi tourism guide.

During the cooler months, both cities are wonderful for parks, beaches, picnics, cycling and outdoor dining.

During summer, family life moves indoors in both locations.

Restaurants and Social Life

Dubai

Dubai has an enormous and constantly changing restaurant scene. You can find everything from inexpensive local favourites to celebrity restaurants and luxury dining experiences.

There is always somewhere new to try, and the city has a very active nightlife and social scene.

If dining out, events and nightlife are a big part of your lifestyle, Dubai offers more variety.

Abu Dhabi

Abu Dhabi also has excellent restaurants, cafés, brunches and hotel dining, but the scene feels smaller and more relaxed.

You may not have the same overwhelming number of new openings, but there are still many fantastic places to discover, especially around Yas Island, Saadiyat, Al Maryah Island, Reem Island and the Corniche.

For us, Abu Dhabi has plenty to enjoy while making it slightly easier to slow down and spend intentional time together.

Living in Abu Dhabi also does not mean giving up everything Dubai offers. We can still enjoy Dubai’s restaurants, events and attractions while returning to the calmer family life we have chosen in Abu Dhabi.

Travel and Airports

Both cities are well positioned for international travel.

Dubai International Airport offers a huge number of global connections. Depending on where you live in Dubai, reaching the airport during heavy traffic can take time.

Abu Dhabi’s Zayed International Airport is modern and well connected, and Etihad Airways provides access to destinations around the world.

Your preferred airline, work travel and the destinations you visit most often may influence which city is more convenient.

The two cities are also close enough for residents to use either airport when the flight options or prices make it worthwhile.

Work and Career Opportunities

Your workplace should play a major role in your decision, but it does not necessarily have to determine where you live.

Dubai has a large and diverse private-sector economy, with opportunities across hospitality, tourism, retail, technology, media, finance, property and many other industries.

Abu Dhabi is the UAE’s capital and has strong opportunities in government, energy, finance, healthcare, education, culture, technology and related sectors.

Living in one city and working in the other is absolutely possible. I do it every working day, and many other UAE residents make the same choice.

The key is to be realistic about the route rather than immediately dismissing the idea. The commute can work particularly well when your home and workplace are both positioned close to the main road between the two cities.

Before committing, drive the full journey during your expected working hours. Also calculate the cost of fuel, tolls, car maintenance and the additional mileage you will add each year.

Most importantly, consider what you gain in return. For our family, living in Abu Dhabi gives us the lifestyle and home environment we want, while commuting allows me to continue working in Dubai. That balance makes the journey worthwhile.

Which City Is Better for Different Families?

Dubai May Suit Your Family If:

  • You enjoy a fast-paced lifestyle.
  • You want the widest possible variety of restaurants and entertainment.
  • You prefer access to the Metro and a larger public transport network.
  • You want to live close to your Dubai workplace.
  • You enjoy constant events, new openings and social opportunities.
  • You want a huge choice of residential communities and schools.
  • You do not mind a busier environment.

Abu Dhabi May Suit Your Family If:

  • You prefer a calmer pace of life.
  • You want a city that feels spacious and family focused.
  • You enjoy beaches, islands and outdoor activities.
  • You prefer less pressure to be constantly busy.
  • You want access to culture, nature and family attractions.
  • You are comfortable relying more heavily on a car.
  • You work in Dubai but are willing to commute for the Abu Dhabi lifestyle.

My Honest Experience

Dubai was my home for more than 12 years. It is where I built my career, raised my daughters and experienced some of the most significant chapters of my life.

I love Dubai’s energy, opportunities and the fact that there is always something happening. It gave me a life I could never have imagined when I first moved to the UAE, and it remains an important part of my life because I still work there.

Moving to Abu Dhabi did not mean walking away from Dubai. Instead, we chose to separate where we wanted to build our family life from where I happened to work.

I now live in Abu Dhabi and commute to Dubai every working day. The journey takes planning, and it adds time and mileage to my day, but it is very doable. I am also far from the only person making this commute.

For me, the drive is a worthwhile exchange for the lifestyle we have in Abu Dhabi. Our home life feels calmer, the pace is more manageable, and the city suits this stage of our family’s life.

At the same time, I can continue my career in Dubai and remain connected to the city that was my home for so many years.

That does not make Abu Dhabi better than Dubai. It makes Abu Dhabi better suited to what our family needs right now and commuting allows me to enjoy the benefits of both cities.

Your answer may be completely different.

Final Verdict

There is no single winner in the Dubai versus Abu Dhabi debate.

Dubai offers energy, choice, convenience and endless entertainment. Abu Dhabi offers space, calm, culture and a more relaxed family rhythm.

You also do not always have to choose between living in one city and working in the other. The daily commute between Abu Dhabi and Dubai is possible, and many people successfully make it part of their routine.

Before deciding:

  1. Confirm the exact location of your workplace.
  2. Research suitable schools.
  3. Compare realistic housing costs.
  4. Test the daily commute during your actual travel times.
  5. Calculate fuel, toll and vehicle costs.
  6. Consider how you want your family’s weekdays and weekends to feel.
  7. Think about whether the benefits of your preferred city make the commute worthwhile.
  8. Visit both cities if possible.

Do not choose a city based only on which one looks more exciting on social media. Choose the place where your family’s ordinary Mondays will work, not only where your weekends will look impressive.

For our family, Abu Dhabi gives us the lifestyle we want, while my daily commute allows me to continue working in Dubai. It may not be the right arrangement for everyone, but it proves that living in one emirate and working in the other can be a realistic and rewarding option.

Whether you choose Dubai, Abu Dhabi or a combination of living in one and working in the other, both cities can offer your family a safe, exciting and rewarding life in the UAE.

School fees, housing prices, transport services and local requirements can change. Confirm current information through the relevant authorities, including KHDA for Dubai schools and ADEK for Abu Dhabi schools.

title: Our Favourite Family Money-Saving Apps in the UAE
content:
Family life in the UAE is full of amazing things to do, but those restaurant meals, beach days, children’s activities and shopping trips can quickly add up. With two girls and a family calendar that always seems to be full, I have learned that saving money is often less about staying home and more about planning our spending properly.

Before we book an activity, reserve a restaurant or plan a pool day, we usually check whether one of our favourite apps can make it more affordable. Sometimes the saving is a buy-one-get-one-free offer. Sometimes it is discounted entry, complimentary access or points that can be used against a future purchase.

These are four of our favourite family money-saving apps and memberships in the UAE: The ENTERTAINER, Fazaa, Privilee and AURA.

They work in different ways, and not every option will suit every family. The secret is knowing what each one does best and using it for spending that was already part of your plans.

1. The ENTERTAINER

The ENTERTAINER is one of the first places we check when planning a family meal, attraction or day out.

It is best known for its buy-one-get-one-free offers, with deals across restaurants, brunches, attractions, activities, spas, salons, fitness venues and hotels. The exact participating venues and offer conditions can change, so we always search the app before deciding where to go.

For families, the savings can be significant. Paying for two children at an attraction or ordering several main meals at a restaurant quickly increases the bill. If the venue has a suitable two-for-one offer, one redemption can sometimes make a noticeable difference to the total cost.

We find it especially useful for:

  • Family meals and casual dining
  • Brunches
  • Children’s attractions and activities
  • Waterparks and theme parks
  • Staycations and hotel experiences
  • Trying somewhere new without paying the full price for everyone

The ENTERTAINER works best when you check it before making plans. Instead of choosing a venue and hoping there is an offer, we often browse the available options first and use them to help us decide where to go.

However, a discount is only a saving if it is something you genuinely wanted. There is no point driving across the UAE or spending more than planned simply because an offer is available.

Our tip for using The ENTERTAINER

Search the exact branch before visiting and read the offer conditions carefully. Some offers may not apply on public holidays, special occasions or certain menu items. If you are unsure, call the venue before booking.

For a family that regularly eats out or visits paid attractions, the membership can often pay for itself surprisingly quickly.

2. Fazaa

Fazaa is one of those apps that is easy to forget about until you remember just how many different areas it can cover.

It is not limited to restaurants and entertainment. Depending on your membership type and the offers available, Fazaa can provide savings across everyday shopping, food and consumer products, travel, hotels, entertainment, healthcare, education, transport and other family-related services.

That variety is what makes it useful for family life. The biggest savings are not always attached to a glamorous day out. Sometimes it is a discount on something practical that we already needed to buy.

We check Fazaa for:

  • Entertainment and attraction tickets
  • Hotel and travel offers
  • Restaurants and food-related discounts
  • Retail purchases
  • Family services and everyday expenses
  • Limited-time promotions

Eligibility and benefits can vary, so families should check which Fazaa membership they qualify for and what is currently included. During the UAE’s Year of the Family 2026, Fazaa also introduced a free discount membership initiative for eligible resident families. As programmes and eligibility rules can change, it is best to apply through the official Fazaa website or app and confirm the current terms.

Our tip for using Fazaa

Do not only open the app when you are planning something expensive. Check it before routine purchases too. Smaller savings used regularly can add up to more than one large discount used once a year.

3. Privilee

Privilee is different from a traditional discount app. It is a paid lifestyle and wellness membership that provides access to participating hotel pools, private beaches, gyms, fitness facilities and selected family-friendly venues across the UAE.

At first glance, the membership cost can seem high. Whether it saves money depends entirely on how often your family will use it.

For families who enjoy regular pool and beach days, Privilee can replace the cost of repeatedly purchasing resort day passes. Selected venues offer family-friendly pools, splash areas, kids’ clubs or waterpark access, although children’s access rules, ages and availability differ by location and membership.

It can also combine family leisure with adult fitness. Rather than paying separately for a gym membership, fitness classes and weekend resort access, one membership may cover several parts of your lifestyle.

We see the greatest value in Privilee for:

  • Regular family pool and beach days
  • Access to participating five-star resorts
  • Gym and fitness access for adults
  • Trying different venues instead of returning to the same hotel
  • Restaurant and spa savings at selected locations
  • Planning easy weekends without booking a full staycation

The real saving comes from frequency. If you only want a hotel pool day once or twice a year, individual day passes will probably make more sense. If your family uses Privilee several times a month, especially during the UAE’s cooler months, the cost per visit can become much more reasonable.

Our tip for using Privilee

Before joining, make a realistic list of the nearby venues you would actually use. Check the children’s access rules, excluded dates, booking requirements and whether your preferred locations are available on the membership you are considering.

Do the calculation based on your normal habits, not your most ambitious version of family life.

4. AURA

AURA is the easiest app on this list to justify because membership is free.

It is Alshaya’s lifestyle rewards programme, allowing members to earn points at participating brands across categories including fashion, beauty, footwear, home and dining. Points can then be redeemed against eligible future purchases or selected rewards.

For our family, AURA is useful because it connects spending across multiple familiar brands. Instead of collecting small amounts of value in several unrelated places, the points build within one programme.

Participating brands and exclusions can change, but the AURA network includes popular names across shopping and dining. The app also features member-only prices, personalised offers, bonus-point opportunities and different membership tiers.

We use AURA for:

  • Collecting points on eligible family shopping
  • Earning rewards when eating at participating restaurants
  • Checking member-only offers before buying
  • Using accumulated points towards future purchases
  • Taking advantage of bonus-point promotions when they match something we already need

Because joining is free, there is very little downside. The main challenge is remembering to scan the app or connect your membership whenever you make an eligible purchase.

Our tip for using AURA

Open the app before shopping rather than afterwards. Check for bonus offers or member prices and make sure your AURA membership is linked when ordering online. Also keep an eye on point expiry dates so the value you have earned is not wasted.

The ENTERTAINER tends to deliver the most obvious immediate saving because you can see the second meal, ticket or experience removed from the bill.

Fazaa can save money across a much wider range of family expenses, including purchases we may already need to make.

Privilee can offer excellent value, but only when it is used regularly. It is the one that requires the most honest calculation before joining.

AURA is the easiest one to keep because it is free and rewards purchases at participating brands without requiring a paid subscription.

How we avoid spending more in the name of saving

Discount apps can be incredibly useful, but they can also tempt us to spend money we had not planned to spend.

Our basic rule is simple: decide what we want to do or buy, then look for a saving. We try not to buy something purely because an app tells us it is discounted.

Before using an offer, we ask:

  • Would we have bought this without the discount?
  • Is the participating venue convenient for us?
  • Are there restrictions that make the offer difficult to use?
  • Does the final price still fit our family budget?
  • Will we realistically use a paid membership often enough?

This turns the apps into budgeting tools rather than excuses to spend.

Small habits can create meaningful savings

Living in the UAE gives families access to an incredible range of restaurants, attractions, resorts and experiences. We do not want to miss out on those things, but we also do not want every family day to place unnecessary pressure on our budget.

The ENTERTAINER, Fazaa, Privilee and AURA help us enjoy more of what the UAE offers while being smarter about what we pay. Some deliver instant discounts, while others create value over time. Used properly, they can reduce the cost of everything from a casual dinner to a full family resort day.

The most important lesson we have learned is to check before paying. A few minutes spent searching the apps can make a genuine difference to the cost of family life, and those savings can be put towards the next meal, day out or memory together.

Offers, memberships, participating venues, eligibility requirements and prices may change. Always check the latest conditions in the relevant app before making a booking or purchase.

title: The Real Cost of Living in the UAE
content:
The UAE is often promoted as a tax-free destination with beautiful homes, excellent schools, year-round sunshine and an incredible lifestyle.

All of that can be true, but living here is not cheap.

When people consider a job offer in the UAE, they often focus on the monthly salary. What they do not always consider is how much they will need to pay upfront for rent, insurance, school fees, deposits and other expenses.

After living in the UAE for more than 13 years, raising children here and experiencing life in both Dubai and Abu Dhabi, I have learned that the cost of living is not simply about how much you earn. It is about how your employment package is structured, where you live, which schools you choose and the kind of lifestyle you want.

Here is an honest look at the real cost of living in the UAE and the expenses you need to consider before accepting a job or moving your family.

Is the UAE Really Tax-Free?

The UAE does not currently impose personal income tax on individuals, which means employees generally receive their salary without personal income tax being deducted.

However, tax-free does not mean expense-free.

The UAE applies 5% VAT to many goods and services. Residents may also pay municipality-related housing charges, road tolls, parking fees, government service charges and other costs depending on where and how they live.

You can find current information about taxation on the official UAE Government portal.

The lack of personal income tax can be a major financial benefit, but only if your salary comfortably covers your living costs and still allows you to save.

Your Employment Package Matters

Two people earning the same salary can have completely different financial experiences depending on their employment benefits.

Before accepting a UAE job offer, ask whether your package includes:

  • Medical insurance
  • Medical insurance for your spouse and children
  • Housing or a housing allowance
  • School fee assistance
  • Annual return flights
  • Relocation expenses
  • Transport or a car allowance
  • Mobile phone allowance
  • End-of-service benefits

A salary that sounds generous may not go very far if you need to pay for rent, two children’s school fees, family medical insurance and annual flights from your salary.

Ask for every benefit to be confirmed in writing. Do not assume that “family status” automatically means all family expenses are covered.

1. Rent and Housing Costs

Rent is likely to be your largest monthly expense.

The amount you pay will depend on:

  • The emirate
  • The neighbourhood
  • The size of the property
  • Whether you choose an apartment or villa
  • The age and condition of the property
  • Community facilities
  • Proximity to schools and work
  • Whether the property is furnished

A studio or one-bedroom apartment in an affordable community will cost far less than a family villa in a premium neighbourhood.

The advertised annual rent is also not the only amount you need to budget for.

Additional housing expenses may include:

  • Security deposit
  • Estate agency commission
  • Tenancy registration
  • Utility deposits
  • Air-conditioning deposits
  • Moving fees
  • Internet installation
  • Furniture and appliances
  • Maintenance
  • Municipality-related housing charges

Rent may be paid in one or several instalments rather than through a standard monthly payment. A landlord may accept multiple cheques, but paying in fewer instalments can sometimes result in a better rental price.

Before signing a contract, make sure you understand how much money you need to provide immediately.

2. Electricity, Water and Air Conditioning

Utility costs vary greatly depending on the size of your home, the season and what is included in your tenancy.

Your regular housing bills may include:

  • Electricity
  • Water
  • Air conditioning
  • Gas
  • Municipality charges
  • Home internet
  • Television packages

Air conditioning is essential for much of the year. In some properties, cooling is included in the rent. In others, it is charged separately through a district cooling provider.

A villa, especially one with a garden or swimming pool, will generally cost more to run than an apartment.

Ask the estate agent or previous tenant for an estimate of summer utility bills before renting a property. A home that appears affordable may become expensive once cooling and maintenance costs are added.

3. School and Nursery Fees

Education can be one of the largest expenses for families living in the UAE.

The country offers many excellent private schools with a wide range of curriculums and fee levels. Annual tuition can vary dramatically between schools and year groups.

Do not look only at the main tuition figure. Ask for the complete list of mandatory and optional fees.

In Dubai, the KHDA School Fees Fact Sheet is designed to show parents the mandatory and optional fees charged by individual schools. Families considering Abu Dhabi schools can use the ADEK school and fee information.

Additional education costs may include:

  • Application fees
  • Assessment fees
  • Registration or re-enrolment fees
  • Deposits
  • Uniforms
  • Shoes and sportswear
  • Books
  • Stationery
  • Laptops or tablets
  • School transport
  • Lunches
  • Educational trips
  • Residential trips
  • Examination fees
  • Graduation fees
  • Class photographs
  • Costumes for performances
  • Charity days and special events

If an employer offers a school allowance, check whether it covers tuition only or whether you can also claim some of the additional mandatory fees.

4. After-School Activities and Sports

This is a major expense that families can easily overlook.

After-school activities and sports are not necessarily included in the school fees. Even when a school offers some free extracurricular clubs, specialist activities and external sports programmes may carry additional term fees.

Your child may want to participate in:

  • Swimming
  • Gymnastics
  • Football
  • Rugby
  • Netball
  • Cricket
  • Tennis
  • Martial arts
  • Dance
  • Music lessons
  • Drama
  • Art classes
  • Coding
  • Academic tutoring

In addition to the lesson or term fee, you may need to pay for:

  • Registration
  • Uniforms
  • Sports kits
  • Shoes
  • Equipment
  • Competition entry
  • Performances
  • Examinations
  • Team travel
  • Private coaching
  • Holiday camps
  • Transport to and from activities

For two or more children, these expenses add up very quickly.

Official Dubai school fee fact sheets show that extracurricular activities can be listed separately from tuition, with the amount varying by school and activity. Some schools also list separate charges for transport, trips, uniforms and annual events.

When creating your family budget, give each child a separate allowance for sports and activities. Do not assume these costs are included in your school payments.

5. Groceries and Household Shopping

Your grocery bill will depend heavily on where you shop and which products you buy.

The UAE has supermarkets catering to many different nationalities. Local products and regional brands can be affordable, while imported products from your home country may cost much more.

Your regular shopping may include:

  • Food
  • Cleaning products
  • Toiletries
  • Bottled or filtered water
  • Lunch-box supplies
  • Pet food
  • Household essentials
  • Delivery charges

Shopping at hypermarkets, buying supermarket brands and using loyalty offers can reduce your bill. Smaller premium supermarkets and imported speciality products will increase it.

One of the easiest ways to overspend is through frequent grocery delivery. Adding a few extra items to several small orders each week can cost much more than one planned shop.

6. Medical Insurance and Healthcare

Medical insurance is essential, but the level of cover varies significantly.

Some employers provide excellent family coverage. Others cover only the employee, leaving the employee responsible for insuring a spouse and children.

If your family is not covered, remember that medical insurance is often paid upfront for the full year. It is not necessarily a small monthly expense.

Before choosing a policy, check:

  • Which hospitals and clinics are included
  • Co-payment amounts
  • Annual limits
  • Dental and optical cover
  • Maternity benefits
  • Prescription medication
  • Existing or chronic conditions
  • Mental health services
  • Emergency treatment
  • Physiotherapy
  • International cover

Even with insurance, you may still need to pay co-payments, deductibles, medication costs and treatments that fall outside your policy.

Keep an emergency medical fund, especially if anyone in the family has an ongoing medical condition.

7. Cars and Transport

Many UAE families find that owning a car makes daily life easier, especially when managing school runs, activities and work commutes.

The cost of a car is not limited to the monthly payment.

You may need to budget for:

  • Deposit or down payment
  • Monthly finance or lease payments
  • Registration
  • Annual insurance
  • Fuel
  • Road tolls
  • Parking
  • Servicing
  • Tyres
  • Repairs
  • Car washing
  • Fines
  • Depreciation

Car insurance is generally paid upfront for the year, so it should be treated as an annual expense rather than a regular monthly bill.

I live in Abu Dhabi and commute to Dubai for work every day. This is very doable and many residents commute between the two emirates, but the additional fuel, tolls, mileage and car maintenance must be included in the household budget.

Public transport can be a more affordable option in some parts of Dubai. However, families living outside Metro-connected areas or in Abu Dhabi may find a car more practical.

8. Mobile Phones and Home Internet

Mobile and internet packages can cost more than new expats expect.

Your monthly communication costs may include:

  • Mobile phone contract
  • Device payment
  • Home internet
  • Television package
  • Streaming services
  • Additional family mobile lines
  • International calling plans

Compare packages carefully and check the contract period before signing. Promotional rates may only apply for the first few months.

If your employer provides a mobile phone or allowance, confirm whether it includes personal use.

9. Home Help and Childcare

Many UAE families employ home help, use cleaning services or pay for childcare.

Options may include:

  • Nursery
  • Day-care
  • Full-time nanny
  • Live-in domestic worker
  • Part-time cleaner
  • Babysitter
  • After-school childcare
  • School holiday camps

If you sponsor a domestic worker yourself, your costs may include more than a monthly salary. Depending on the arrangement, you may also be responsible for:

  • Visa and residency costs
  • Medical testing
  • Emirates ID
  • Health insurance
  • Flights
  • Accommodation
  • Food
  • Agency or recruitment fees
  • End-of-service obligations

If you use an agency or hourly service, compare the total monthly cost with your actual needs.

Childcare expenses often increase during school holidays, when parents may need holiday camps, babysitters or additional nanny support.

10. Dining Out and Entertainment

The UAE offers something for every budget, from affordable local restaurants and free beaches to luxury brunches, resorts and premium attractions.

It is very easy for entertainment spending to grow without noticing.

Regular lifestyle expenses may include:

  • Restaurants
  • Takeaway and food delivery
  • Coffee
  • Brunches
  • Children’s attractions
  • Cinemas
  • Theme parks
  • Beach clubs
  • Gym memberships
  • Salons and beauty treatments
  • Weekend staycations
  • Concerts and events
  • Birthday parties
  • Gifts

A single family visit to a major attraction can be expensive once tickets, food, parking and souvenirs are included.

You do not have to give up enjoying the UAE. Plan your entertainment budget and balance major attractions with parks, beaches, community events and free activities. You can also look into purchasing annual passes for theme parks and attractions which often work out a cheaper option and provides entertainment for the family for the whole year. As we live in Abu Dhabi we have an annual pass to all the theme parks on Yas Island. 

11. Flights and Travel

Many expat families want to visit their home countries at least once a year.

Flights during school holidays can be extremely expensive, especially for a family. If your employer provides only one annual ticket or covers the employee but not dependants, the remaining cost will come from your household budget.

Include:

  • Flights
  • Baggage
  • Airport transfers
  • Pet boarding
  • Travel insurance
  • Accommodation
  • Spending money
  • Visas for international destinations

Divide your expected annual travel cost by 12 and save that amount each month.

Living in the UAE also makes short international trips and staycations very tempting. These experiences are wonderful, but they need their own place in the budget.

12. Pets

Moving with or adopting a pet brings additional costs.

These may include:

  • Import permits
  • Relocation services
  • Vaccinations
  • Microchipping
  • Annual registration
  • Veterinary care
  • Food
  • Grooming
  • Boarding
  • Pet sitting
  • Training
  • Deposits or restrictions on rental properties

Veterinary emergencies can be expensive, so consider pet insurance or a dedicated emergency fund.

13. Upfront and Annual Expenses

One of the biggest differences between budgeting in the UAE and budgeting in some other countries is the number of large expenses that may need to be paid upfront.

These can include:

  • Rental payments
  • Security deposit
  • Estate agency commission
  • School fees
  • School registration
  • Medical insurance
  • Car insurance
  • Car registration
  • Annual flights
  • Visa renewals
  • Club memberships
  • Sports and after-school activity fees

A family may appear comfortable based on monthly spending but struggle when several annual payments fall due at the same time.

Create a separate savings account for annual expenses. Add up the total amount you expect to pay during the year, divide it by 12 and transfer that amount every month.

Hidden Costs New Expats Often Overlook

Some of the expenses that may surprise new residents include:

  • Document attestation
  • Visa costs for dependants
  • Temporary accommodation
  • Rental deposits
  • Estate agency fees
  • Utility deposits
  • Air-conditioning charges
  • Furniture and appliances
  • School registration fees
  • Uniforms and devices
  • After-school activities
  • Holiday camps
  • Annual insurance payments
  • Road tolls and parking
  • Car maintenance
  • International school trips
  • Family flights
  • Pet relocation
  • Home maintenance
  • Birthday parties and gifts
  • Work clothing
  • Delivery fees
  • Subscriptions

None of these may seem enormous on its own, but together they can have a major effect on your finances.

These sample budgets are broad planning examples, not fixed prices. Your actual costs may be lower or considerably higher depending on your emirate, housing, school, lifestyle and employment benefits.

How Much Salary Do You Need?

There is no single salary that guarantees a comfortable life in the UAE.

A good salary for a single person may not be enough for a family with two children in private school. A family receiving housing, education and medical benefits may be more comfortable than a family earning a higher salary without those benefits.

Before accepting an offer, calculate:

  1. Your guaranteed monthly income.
  2. Your annual employment benefits.
  3. Your estimated housing costs.
  4. Your children’s complete education costs.
  5. Your annual insurance expenses.
  6. Your transport costs.
  7. Your normal lifestyle spending.
  8. The amount you want to save each month.
  9. The cost of visiting your home country.
  10. Your emergency fund contribution.

If the budget only works when nothing goes wrong, the salary may not be enough.

My Best Budgeting Advice

The UAE can offer an incredible quality of life, but it is also a place where lifestyle spending can grow very quickly.

My best advice is to create three separate budgets:

Monthly Living Costs

This should cover rent provision, utilities, groceries, transport and daily household expenses.

Annual Expenses

This should cover insurance, school payments, flights, registrations, activities and other large annual bills.

Savings and Emergencies

This should include emergency savings, long-term savings and money for unexpected travel or medical expenses.

Do not build your lifestyle around every dirham you earn. Leave room for emergencies, job changes and the possibility that your circumstances may change.

Final Thoughts

The UAE can be a wonderful place to build a career, raise a family and create a life filled with opportunities.

However, the lifestyle you see on social media does not show the school invoices, insurance renewals, rental cheques and other responsibilities happening in the background.

Before moving, look beyond the headline salary. Calculate the real cost of the life your family wants to live and make sure your employment package supports it.

You do not need a luxury budget to enjoy the UAE. Some of our best family days involve beaches, parks, picnics and discovering places close to home. What matters is creating a lifestyle that you can genuinely afford without feeling under constant financial pressure.

Plan carefully, ask the right questions and remember that being financially comfortable is more valuable than simply looking successful.

Always request current prices directly from schools, insurers, landlords and service providers before making financial decisions.

title: Moving to the UAE: Everything You Need to Know Before You Go
author: Donne
content:
Moving to the UAE can be one of the most exciting decisions you will ever make, but it can also feel completely overwhelming.

When I first moved here more than 13 years ago, I had no idea how much my life would change. Since then, I have built a career, raised my children, experienced life in both Dubai and Abu Dhabi and created a home for our beautifully blended family.

The UAE offers incredible opportunities, a high standard of living, year-round sunshine and a wonderfully international community. However, moving here involves much more than packing your suitcase and booking a flight.

From visas and housing to schools, healthcare and everyday expenses, here is what you should know before beginning your new life in the UAE.

1. Research the Different Emirates

The United Arab Emirates is made up of seven emirates, and each one offers a different lifestyle.

Dubai is fast-paced, energetic and filled with restaurants, attractions, events and career opportunities. Abu Dhabi feels slightly calmer and more spacious while still offering beautiful beaches, excellent schools, family communities and plenty to do.

Sharjah, Ajman, Ras Al Khaimah, Fujairah and Umm Al Quwain can offer a quieter lifestyle and, depending on the area, more affordable housing. However, you must consider where you will work, your daily commute and where your children will attend school.

Do not choose an area based on photographs alone. Look at traffic during your expected commuting times, nearby schools, supermarkets, medical facilities and the general feel of the community.

2. Understand Your Visa Situation

Before moving, make sure you understand exactly which visa you will have and who will be responsible for arranging it.

Many expats move to the UAE with an employment visa sponsored by their employer. Other options may include family sponsorship, investor visas, freelance permits, remote-working visas and longer-term residence programmes.

If you are relocating for a job, your employer should provide an official employment offer and explain the visa process. Be cautious of anyone asking you to pay large amounts of money in exchange for a job or work visa. The UAE Government provides guidance on avoiding labour and visa fraud.

Adults applying for UAE residence will usually need to complete medical screening. Once your residency process is complete, you will receive an Emirates ID, which becomes one of your most important forms of identification in the country.

Visa requirements can change, so always check the latest information on the official UAE Government website or with the relevant emirate’s immigration authority.

3. Prepare and Attest Your Documents

Do not leave your paperwork until the last minute.

Depending on your employment and family circumstances, you may need original or officially attested copies of documents such as:

  • Marriage certificate
  • Children’s birth certificates
  • University degrees and professional qualifications
  • School reports and transfer certificates
  • Vaccination and medical records
  • Driving licence records
  • Divorce or custody documents, where applicable
  • Passport copies and passport photographs

The documents required and the attestation process will depend on the country where they were issued and what they will be used for in the UAE.

Ask your employer, school or relevant government authority exactly what is required before paying for attestation. Bringing the correct documents with you can save weeks of stress after you arrive.

4. Look Closely at Your Employment Package

A UAE salary can look attractive, but the full employment package matters just as much as the amount you receive each month.

Before accepting a role, ask whether the package includes:

  • Medical insurance
  • Family medical insurance
  • Housing or a housing allowance
  • School fee assistance
  • Annual return flights
  • Relocation support
  • Transport or a car allowance
  • Mobile phone allowance
  • End-of-service benefits

Read your employment contract carefully and make sure it matches the offer you accepted. If something was promised during the interview process, ask for it to be included in writing.

The UAE does not currently impose personal income tax on individuals, but that does not mean living here is inexpensive. The country applies VAT to many goods and services, and large expenses such as rent, education and healthcare must be considered when evaluating your salary. You can check current tax information through the official UAE Government portal.

5. Calculate the Real Cost of Living

The cost of living in the UAE varies dramatically depending on your lifestyle, family size, chosen emirate and preferred neighbourhood.

Your biggest expenses are likely to include:

  • Rent and housing deposits
  • School and nursery fees
  • Utilities and air conditioning
  • Groceries
  • Medical insurance
  • Transport
  • Car payments and insurance
  • Mobile phone and internet
  • Home help or childcare
  • Entertainment and dining out

When you first arrive, you may also need money for temporary accommodation, furniture, deposits, agency fees, school registration fees and setting up utilities.

Try to arrive with an emergency fund rather than relying on your first salary. Setting up a new life almost always costs more than expected.

6. Do Not Rush into Choosing a Home

It can be tempting to sign for the first beautiful apartment or villa you see, especially when you are tired of living in temporary accommodation.

Take your time.

In addition to the rent, ask about:

  • Security deposit
  • Agency commission
  • Number and timing of rental payments
  • Maintenance responsibilities
  • Air-conditioning charges
  • Parking
  • Community fees
  • Nearby construction
  • Traffic during rush hour
  • Distance from work and school
  • Supermarkets and facilities within the area

A home that looks affordable may become expensive once additional costs are included. It is also worth visiting the community during both the day and evening before making a decision.

One of the biggest lessons I have learned is that your daily commute can have a huge effect on your quality of life. A slightly more expensive home closer to work or school may be worth it if it gives you more time with your family.

7. Research Schools Early

If you are moving with children, start researching schools as soon as possible.

The UAE has a wide choice of international schools offering British, American, IB, Australian, Indian and other curriculums. Fees, facilities, inspection ratings, locations and availability vary significantly.

Think about:

  • Which curriculum your child currently follows
  • Whether you may return to your home country
  • School fees and additional charges
  • Distance from home and work
  • Transport options
  • Class sizes
  • After-school activities
  • Support for children with additional needs
  • Waiting lists and application deadlines

Book school tours where possible and speak to other parents, but remember that every child is different. A school that is perfect for one family may not be the right environment for another.

You may need previous school reports, vaccination records, identification documents and an official transfer certificate, so confirm the requirements directly with each school.

8. Understand Healthcare and Insurance

The UAE has excellent public and private healthcare, but treatment can be expensive without appropriate insurance.

Health insurance requirements and coverage can vary between emirates and employers. Check whether your employer covers only you or your entire family. If your family is not covered consider that medical insurance payments are made upfront for the entire year and is not a monthly expense so budget for that separately. 

Before accepting an insurance plan, look at:

  • Which hospitals and clinics are included
  • Whether dental and optical treatment are covered
  • Maternity benefits
  • Existing or chronic medical conditions
  • Prescription medication
  • Emergency treatment
  • Annual limits and co-payments

If you take regular medication, bring enough for your first few weeks and check whether it is available and permitted in the UAE. Keep medication in its original packaging and carry a copy of your prescription or doctor’s letter when necessary.

9. Decide How You Will Get Around

Public transport is excellent in some parts of the UAE, particularly Dubai, but many families eventually choose to drive.

Your ability to exchange your existing driving licence will depend on where it was issued and the current rules. Some nationalities can convert their licences, while others must complete driving lessons and tests.

If you plan to buy or lease a car, include the cost of registration, insurance, fuel, parking and road tolls in your budget. Car insurance is also charged upfront for the year. 

Also consider your commute before choosing where to live. A location that appears close on a map can take much longer to reach during peak traffic.

10. Prepare for the Climate

The UAE is known for sunshine, but the summer heat can be a shock if you have never experienced it before.

From roughly May to September, temperatures and humidity can become intense. Life continues, but routines change. Outdoor activities move to early mornings or evenings, and families spend more time at indoor attractions, shopping centres and pools.

Pack lightweight, breathable clothing, but bring a cardigan or light jacket because indoor air conditioning can be surprisingly cold.

Hydration, sunscreen and car safety are especially important during summer. Never leave children or pets unattended in a vehicle, even for a moment.

11. Learn About Local Culture

The UAE is modern and welcoming, with people from almost every part of the world. It is also a Muslim country with local traditions and laws that residents and visitors are expected to respect.

Dress requirements are generally relaxed in many areas, but modest clothing is appropriate in government buildings, places of worship and more traditional locations.

During Ramadan, be considerate of those who are fasting and pay attention to local guidance around eating, drinking, working hours and public behaviour.

Also be mindful when taking photographs. Do not photograph people without permission, particularly families and children.

You do not need to know everything before arriving. A respectful attitude, willingness to learn and basic awareness of local customs will take you a long way.

12. Prepare Yourself Emotionally

Moving abroad is not only a practical change. It is an emotional one too.

The excitement of a new home can sit alongside homesickness, loneliness and uncertainty. You may miss family, familiar food, old routines and the feeling of knowing exactly how everything works.

Building a new support network takes time. Join community groups, speak to other parents, attend local events and accept invitations when you can. Some of the strongest friendships I have made began because we were all far from home and trying to find our place.

If your children are moving with you, allow them to feel excited, nervous, sad or even angry. Include them in decisions where possible and help them stay connected with the people they love back home.

13. Expect the First Few Months to Feel Unsettled

Your first few weeks may be filled with paperwork, appointments, property viewings, school applications and trips to places you cannot find without your phone.

This is normal.

You will eventually know which supermarket has your favourite products, which delivery app is the fastest and which route avoids the worst traffic. The unfamiliar gradually becomes familiar.

Give yourself time to adjust before deciding whether you love or hate your new life. Moving countries is a huge transition, and it takes more than a few weeks to feel settled.

Your UAE Moving Checklist

Before you leave, try to have the following organised:

  • Valid passports with sufficient validity
  • Confirmed visa or sponsorship information
  • Written employment offer and contract
  • Attested personal and professional documents
  • School records and transfer certificates
  • Medical and vaccination records
  • Temporary accommodation
  • Health insurance information
  • Emergency savings
  • Digital and printed copies of important documents
  • A plan for transport from the airport
  • A shortlist of suitable homes and schools

Final Thoughts

Moving to the UAE can feel like stepping into the unknown, but it can also open the door to experiences and opportunities you never imagined.

More than 13 years after making the move, the UAE is not simply the place where I live. It is where I have raised my girls, built my career, experienced enormous personal changes and created a new chapter with my husband and our blended family.

There will be adjustments, frustrating days and moments when you miss home. There will also be new friendships, incredible experiences and the possibility of building a life that feels completely your own.

Prepare as much as you can, stay open-minded and give yourself time. Before long, the place that once felt so unfamiliar may begin to feel like home too.

Please note: Visa, residency, employment and government requirements can change. Always confirm current information through the official UAE Government portal or the appropriate authority before making decisions.

content:
If you are planning to move to the UAE with your family, one of the biggest decisions you may face is whether to live in Dubai or Abu Dhabi.

Both cities offer excellent schools, beautiful beaches, safe communities, modern healthcare and plenty of family activities. However, the experience of living in each city can feel very different.

After living in Dubai for more than 12 years, I recently moved to Abu Dhabi with my husband and daughters. However, I still work in Dubai and commute between the two cities every working day.

This may sound like a huge journey to someone new to the UAE, but commuting between Abu Dhabi and Dubai is very doable. Many people live in one emirate and work in the other. Whether the commute works for you will depend heavily on where you live, where you work and the times you need to travel.

Dubai was my home for a very long time, and it will always be an important part of my story. Abu Dhabi is now where we have chosen to build our family life, while Dubai remains a major part of my professional life.

So, which city is better for your family?

The honest answer is that it depends on the lifestyle you want, your budget, your children’s schools and how your family feels about commuting.

Dubai and Abu Dhabi at a Glance

If your family wants...

Abu Dhabi

To live in Abu Dhabi while continuing a Dubai career

Both, with a daily commute

This is only a general guide. Your experience will depend heavily on the neighbourhood you choose. Some parts of Dubai feel quiet and suburban, while some areas of Abu Dhabi are busy, lively and full of activity.

The Overall Lifestyle

Living in Dubai

Dubai is exciting, ambitious and always moving.

There is constantly a new restaurant opening, an event happening or an attraction to visit. The city is filled with people from around the world, and it can feel as though everything you could possibly need is available.

For families who enjoy being busy, exploring new places and having endless entertainment options, Dubai can be incredible.

However, the pace can also feel intense. Traffic, commuting, busy calendars and the pressure to keep up with everything happening around you can become tiring.

Dubai is a city where it is very easy to be constantly doing something.

Living in Abu Dhabi

Abu Dhabi feels calmer, more spacious and slightly more relaxed.

It is still a modern international city with restaurants, shopping centres, schools, attractions and beautiful hotels, but the overall pace feels less rushed.

Since moving to Abu Dhabi, I have noticed that family life feels a little slower. There is more of a sense that you can step back, breathe and enjoy your surroundings without feeling that you are missing out on ten other things.

That does not mean Abu Dhabi is boring. Yas Island, Saadiyat Island, Hudayriyat Island, the Corniche and the city’s cultural attractions provide plenty to do. The difference is that the city generally feels less hectic.

I now live in Abu Dhabi and commute to Dubai every working day. The journey takes planning, and it adds time and mileage to my day, but it is very doable. I am also far from the only person making this commute.

For me, the drive is a worthwhile exchange for the lifestyle we have in Abu Dhabi. Our home life feels calmer, the pace is more manageable, and the city suits this stage of our family’s life.

At the same time, I can continue my career in Dubai and remain connected to the city that was my home for so many years.

That does not make Abu Dhabi better than Dubai. It makes Abu Dhabi better suited to what our family needs right now and commuting allows me to enjoy the benefits of both cities.

Your answer may be completely different.

Final Verdict

There is no single winner in the Dubai versus Abu Dhabi debate.

Dubai offers energy, choice, convenience and endless entertainment. Abu Dhabi offers space, calm, culture and a more relaxed family rhythm.

You also do not always have to choose between living in one city and working in the other. The daily commute between Abu Dhabi and Dubai is possible, and many people successfully make it part of their routine.

Before deciding:

  1. Confirm the exact location of your workplace.
  2. Research suitable schools.
  3. Compare realistic housing costs.
  4. Test the daily commute during your actual travel times.
  5. Calculate fuel, toll and vehicle costs.
  6. Consider how you want your family’s weekdays and weekends to feel.

For our family, Abu Dhabi gives us the lifestyle we want, while my daily commute allows me to continue working in Dubai. It may not be the right arrangement for everyone, but it proves that living in one emirate and working in the other can be a realistic and rewarding option.

Whether you choose Dubai, Abu Dhabi or a combination of living in one and working in the other, both cities can offer your family a safe, exciting and rewarding life in the UAE.
